title: MA9-13309
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The female claimant, XXXXXXXXX, is a Rwandan citizen. She is claiming refugee protection in Canada as a refugee, under section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA), and as a person in need of protection, under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

Her claim was heard jointly with those filed by her four minor children, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX and XXXXXXXX, for whom she was appointed designated representative, and with the claim filed by her half-sister, XXXXXXXXXX, all of whom are Rwandan citizens. XXXXXXXXXXX Alleged facts
The female claimant alleged the following:

Since 2002, she had operated a business that XXXXXXXXXX. She became a XXXX and a member of the XXXXXXXXXXXXXX in 2009. She was planning on opening her own XXXXX in XXXXX 2010. In 2001, she married a rich merchant. She was a victim of domestic violence. She alleged that the police did not take her complaints into consideration. The children suffered. Her husband told her that he would kill her if she asked him for a divorce. The last beating was on XXXXXX, 2009. Her husband spent two nights in police custody. She did not want to get back together with him afterwards. Her husband was prohibited from going near the house. He complied with the order and did not return to the house, but he nevertheless threatened to kill the claimant over the telephone.

In XXXXX 2009, the claimant and her half-sister, co-claimant XXXXXXXXXXX, helped the authorities catch XXX corrupt XXXXXXXXX who had been demanding bribes, in relation to the female claimant's business. They alleged that these XXXXXXXXX were imprisoned for XXX months. After they were released, the female claimant received [translation] "anonymous" calls in which she was threatened, including threats that she would be killed, which she attributed to these people. On XXXXXXXX, 2009, the female claimant, along with co-claimant XXXXXXXX, was attacked as she was leaving XXXXX; she escaped thanks to a cousin who was passing and some neighbours who intervened. The police opened an investigation. The female claimant had visas for Canada that she and her husband had obtained for her entire family for a trip planned previously. She thus decided to use them to flee the country. Analysis
The female claimant's identity was established to my satisfaction through her testimony and the evidence submitted; her children's were, as well.

The female claimant's husband was a rich businessman in XXXX. The female claimant and her husband had planned a trip to Canada with their children. The husband already had a visa. Together, the spouses completed the necessary formalities and obtained visas for the female claimant and their children on XXXXXXXX, 2009. The trip was planned for XXXXXXXX, 2009.

Things went wrong on XXXXXX, 2009, when the female claimant's husband beat her. Consequently, he was detained by the police for two nights. The female claimant decided to leave her husband. She remained at the house until XXXXXXX, 2009. Her husband did not return. She XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX before she left the country. She admitted that she had decided not to return.

The female claimant produced two exhibits from the Rwanda National Police: 1) an attestation dated XXXX, 2009, confirming that the female claimant had played a [translation] "role in the investigation" that had led to the arrest of certain "Rwanda Revenue Autority2" employees on XXXXXX, 2009; and 2) an attestation dated XXXXXXX, 2009, indicating that the female claimant had often filed complaints about domestic violence, particularly at the time of the assault on XXXXXXX, 2009. It should be added that the officers mediated, often with good results, but for the last incident, the matter was referred to the court.3
It therefore seems clear according to Exhibit C-10 that the female claimant had indeed participated in the investigation that resulted in the arrest of corrupt XXXXXXXX in XXXXX 2009.

It is also clear according to Exhibit C-11 that the female claimant had reconciled with her husband several times prior to the incident on XXXXXX, 2009. This was also confirmed by the fact that, just before that date, they were planning to travel to Canada together with their children.

Exhibit C-11 also makes it clear that the police were not indifferent to the female claimant's hardships and that they intervened several times. Moreover, the female claimant admitted in her narrative that the police also intervened at the time of the attack on XXXXXXXX, 2009, when the female claimant and her half-sister were attacked by unknown individuals as they were leaving the XXX and that the police opened an investigation, even though the attackers had not been identified.

On XXXXXXXX, 2009, the female claimant and her half-sister were leaving the female claimant's XXXX after it had closed, at around 10:00 p.m., when two men suddenly appeared and immediately began to beat them. They had not noticed the female claimant's cousin, who had been following the two women, and he fought the attackers. This happened quickly, according to the female claimant. Then, some people intervened, and the attackers fled. The police arrived. Only the cousin had been injured. He was treated at the hospital.

In her explanations, the female claimant vaguely linked this incident on XXXXXXX, 2009, to some individuals who had gone into the XXX in the preceding days and talked to her half-sister, XXXXX, in her absence.

XXXXXXXX, the co-claimant, testified that twice, about three days before the incident on XXXXXXX, 2009, unknown individuals had gone into the XXXX while XXXXX was absent and had asked to see her. The first time, there was just one visitor, who left his name and telephone number. The next day, two visitors, including the first one, showed up. They again left their names and telephone numbers. They said that they wanted to see XXXXX for money. XXXXX stated that she told XXXXX about this. She also stated that she did not know these people. Presumably, the claimants would have recognized the names if the visitors were the people who had been convicted in XXXXX 2009.

When questioned, XXXXX answered that she did not remember them. Why not? Because she did not know them, she stated. She then tried to give an explanation by referring to the trap that had been set for the public servants, in cooperation with the police, which led her attorney to point out to her that she was confusing the most recent incidents in XXXXXX 2009 with those in XXXX 2009. The female claimant was visibly annoyed and finished by stating that she did not remember the visit by these men in XXXXXX 2009 or XXXXX mentioning it to her. When asked again, XXXXX repeated that these visits had taken place a few days before XXXXXXX, 2009, and that she had told XXXXX about them.

The confusion of the female claimant, XXXXXXXXXX, is surprising, as is the apparent contradiction between her testimony and that of the co-claimant XXXXXXXXX. No satisfactory explanation for this was given.

However, it became apparent in further testimony from XXXXX that she wanted to see a connection between the attack against them on XXXXXXXX, 2009, and the XXXXXXXX that she had helped the police to capture in XXXX 2009. It seems that her confusion might have resulted from her desire to make this connection.

At the hearing, the two claimants stated that they had not recognized the attackers on XXXXXXX, 2009. It can be assumed that they would have recognized them if they were the people who had demanded bribes from them and whom they had helped the police to trap in XXXXXX 2009. It can also be assumed that XXXXX would have recognized them if these were the same people who had come to see her a few days before XXXXXXXX, 2009.

The female claimant XXXXXXXXX added at the hearing that she had heard her attackers say that they had lost their jobs because of them and that they were getting revenge. In her opinion, that demonstrates that the perpetrators of the attack were the people who had been caught at the beginning of the year.

In her written narrative, the female claimant stated, [translation] "Unfortunately, our attackers were not identified." She added that she could not distinguish whether this murder attempt had been ordered by her ex-husband or by the former soldiers.

When it was pointed out to her that that does not match the statements that she had allegedly heard, she answered that it had come into her mind, in her confusion, that the former soldiers (public servants) might have been in collusion with her husband. The panel does not accept that weak and opportune explanation, and it does not find credible the female claimant's testimony regarding the statements she allegedly heard her attackers make.

The panel concludes that the female claimant did not demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that she was attacked on XXXXXXX, 2009, by people whom she had helped the police to capture at the beginning of the year or by her husband. The perpetrator could have been any criminal.

As for her husband, the evidence establishes that he did not bother the female claimant after the incident on XXXXXX, 2009, aside from the telephone threats mentioned by the female claimant. He did not return to pick up any other belongings from their home, and she remained there until XXXXXXX, 2009, taking the time to get wind up her own affairs and liquidate her business. She explained that he is rich and could buy anything he needed and relocate, without having to return to the home to collect his things. There were no other incidents during that period.

In light of all this, the panel is of the opinion that the evidence does not establish that there is a serious possibility that the female claimant would be persecuted today in Rwanda for any of the reasons set out in section 96 of the Act, or that there is a probability of a personal risk or danger everywhere in the country, under section 97 of the Act.

As for state protection, the evidence establishes that the police intervened several times when asked to do so. It was the female claimant herself who had agreed to reconcile, to the point that she had even planned a trip to Canada with her husband and her children prior to the incident on XXXXXX, 2009. At that time, the police intervened again, and in an effective manner according to the evidence. The panel is therefore of the opinion that the presumption that the state can provide adequate protection has not been rebutted.

Finally, as for the Chairperson's Guideline on women who fear gender-related persecution, the panel finds nothing that could have an impact on the assessment of the facts introduced into evidence or on the procedure and that could lead to a different conclusion. Conclusion

Given all these facts and for all these reasons, the panel determines that the female claimant, XXXXXXXX, is not a "Convention" refugee or a "person in need of protection" and rejects her refugee protection claim.

The panel also rejects the refugee protection claim filed by the four children of the female claimant, XXXXXXXXX, on the ground that these claims are derived from the female claimant's and have the same basis. Therefore, the outcome for them must be the same.

The co-claimant, XXXXXXXX, is a Rwandan citizen. She is claiming refugee protection in Canada as a refugee, under section 96 of the IRPA, and as a person in need of protection under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.
Her claim was heard jointly with the claim filed by her half-sister, XXXXXXXX, and her four minor children, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX and XXXXXXXXX. Alleged facts
The co-claimant alleged the following:

Since 2006, she had worked part-time in her half-sister's XXXXXX and had studied at XXXXXXXXXXX University. She stated that in XXXX 2009, soldiers who worked as inspectors for the "XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX" demanded a bribe from her half-sister to XXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXX. The police intervened, and with the cooperation of the two claimants, these people were fired and sentenced to XXXXXX in prison. After they were released, the female claimant and her half-sister started receiving threatening telephone calls.

For the rest, the co-claimant stated that her claim is based on the same facts as those raised by her half-sister, XXXXXXXXX, and that her fears are the same. She added that she was threatened by her half-sister's husband after the couple separated because he blamed her for being complicit with her half-sister. She left the country after her half-sister, by means of a visa that she had obtained in XXXX 2009 for a trip to the United States. She fears returning to Rwanda for the same reasons as her half-sister. Analysis
The co-claimant's identity was established to my satisfaction through her testimony and the evidence submitted.

The facts raised to support her claim are substantially the same as the facts that were raised by her half-sister. Thus, the observations and conclusions in the previous analysis, relating to the claim filed by XXXXXXXXX, also apply to the claim filed by XXXXXXXXX. Conclusion

Given all these facts and for all these reasons, the panel determines that the co-claimant, XXXXXXXXX, is not a "Convention" refugee or a "person in need of protection," and her refugee protection claim is rejected.
